verdict.reasoning: Patient describes room spinning, unsteadiness, ear buzzing, and nausea: "my room is sort of spinning and I can't walk properly... my ears are buzzing a bit... No, but I am feeling very sick. Doctor: Nausea."
Onset about 2 hours ago: "Started probably about two hours ago maybe" and doctor confirms "So it's there now for the past two hours, you'd say?" Patient: "Yeah."
Previous similar episode one month ago lasting 5–10 minutes: "I had it a similar sort of thing about a month ago..." and "Probably only about five, ten minutes."
Continuous since onset: "Yeah, it's there the whole time." and doctor: "So it's there now for the past two hours, you'd say?" Patient: "Yeah."
No vomiting: "Have you been physically sick?" Patient: "No, but I am feeling very sick."
No fever reported: "Do you have a temperature at all?" Patient: "I don't think so."
No recent viral illness: "Did you have any kind of viral illness in the recent past. Past couple of weeks?" Patient: "No." and "No cold, cough, nothing?" Patient: "No, I've been pretty healthy."
No ear pain or discharge: "Any kind of ear pain or ear discharge, anything like that?" Patient: "No, nothing."
Hearing intact aside from buzzing: "It's just a bit of a buzzy noise in my ears, but otherwise I can hear everything."
No limb weakness: "my legs and arms and everything are working fine..." and doctor: "So there's no weakness of your arms and legs?" (implied agreement).
History of premature ovarian failure: Patient: "I've had premature ovarian failure and I've taken hrt."
On hormone replacement therapy: Patient: "I've had premature ovarian failure and I've taken hrt." and doctor: "Okay. HRT and premature ovarian failure."
No known allergies: "Do you have any allergies at all?" Patient: "No."

Acute vertigo with suspected labyrinthitis: doctor describes dizziness/room spinning and states "the most common, you know, diagnosis we would. You're suffering from at the moment is something called labyrinthitis."
Nausea associated with vertigo: "No, but I am feeling very sick." Doctor labels it: "Nausea." in the context of dizziness.

Semitol 1 tablet TID for 10 days to Lloyd Pharmacy: "It's called semitol. Yep. It's one tablet three times a day. So I'll give you about 10 days worth" and "we'll send you across that prescription... Lloyd Pharmacy... Is that correct? Patient: "Yeah."

Paracetamol is mentioned only as an analogy, not as advice for this patient: "This is like, just symptomatic relief. Like, if you have a fever, we just give paracetamol." No explicit instruction to use paracetamol is given.

Advice that it can be taken with or without food: Patient asks about taking with food; doctor: "It doesn't really matter. You can take it because sometimes... you feel a bit sick to eat anything, so might as well just take the tablets."

Plan for face-to-face review including ear exam, BP, and gait/neurologic check: "I would still like you to be seen by one of our doctors to take a look inside your ears... While you're with the doctors, we'd like to do your blood pressure, just examine your, you know, you know, how you're walking, and everything is."

Safety-net advice: "if you develop any weakness of your legs or arms or, you know, a sudden headache, any of those symptoms, or you start being violently sick with it, then, you know, you would need to take yourself to A and E."
Instruction to call support to book appointment: "Just make sure you call support to book that appointment. Okay?"
